keyTakeaways: Hot partitions are the killer at scale, coalesce duplicate reads
ScyllaDB (C++) avoids JVM GC pauses that plagued Cassandra
A request-coalescing data service layer smooths spikes
Rust data services in front of the DB
summary: Discord outgrew Cassandra (GC pauses, hot partitions, maintenance pain) and migrated its trillions of messages to ScyllaDB, a C++ rewrite of Cassandra. They added intermediary "data services" in Rust to coalesce concurrent requests for the same data, taming hot partitions.
title: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages

keyTakeaways: Choose a shard key that matches your access pattern
Bucket by channel + time for range scans
Cassandra for write-heavy, append-only data
Idempotency via monotonic Snowflake IDs
summary: The original story: Discord moved from MongoDB to Cassandra for messages, choosing a schema partitioned by (channel_id, time bucket) so a channel's messages stay together and are efficiently range-scanned. A great primer on picking a shard key.
title: How Discord Stores Billions of Messages

keyTakeaways: Actor model (BEAM) for millions of stateful connections
A single hot process becomes the bottleneck, parallelize fan-out
Read-mostly global state needs special handling
summary: Discord's realtime fan-out runs on Elixir/Erlang's actor model. They hit limits when a huge guild caused a single process to fall behind, and fixed it with a "manifold" for parallel fan-out and Erlang's fastglobal for hot read-mostly data.
title: How Discord Scaled Elixir to 5,000,000 Concurrent Users

keyTakeaways: Encode time + shard + sequence into a 64-bit ID
Time-sortable IDs avoid a central ID service
Logical shards mapped to physical DBs allow rebalancing
summary: Instagram needed globally-unique, roughly time-sortable IDs across a sharded Postgres fleet without a central coordinator. Their answer: 64-bit IDs built from a timestamp + shard id + per-shard sequence, generated inside Postgres with a stored procedure.
title: Sharding & IDs at Instagram

keyTakeaways: Append-only immutable cells simplify replication & auditing
Layer a KV abstraction over sharded MySQL
Trigger-based derived indexes and change feeds
summary: Uber built "Schemaless", an append-only, sharded key-value store layered on top of many MySQL instances, to get horizontal write scale and operational simplicity while keeping MySQL's reliability. Data is stored as immutable cells; buffered writes and triggers drive derived data.
title: Designing Schemaless, Uber's Scalable Datastore Using MySQL

keyTakeaways: Postgres rewrites every index on any update (write amplification)
InnoDB's clustered index + secondary indexes via primary key
Replication format matters at scale
summary: A famously controversial deep-dive: Uber hit Postgres pain points (write amplification from its index/tuple model, replication inefficiency, connection overhead) and moved to MySQL/InnoDB. A must-read on how storage-engine internals affect scale.
title: Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL

keyTakeaways: Idempotency keys make retries safe
Stash the request + response so replays return the same result
Separate the idempotency layer from business logic
summary: Airbnb built idempotency into their payments layer so network retries never charge a guest twice. They use client-supplied idempotency keys, a stateful request-stashing store, and careful transaction boundaries to make retries safe.
title: Avoiding Double Payments in a Distributed Payments System

keyTakeaways: Erasure coding cuts storage cost vs full replication
Immutable content-addressed blocks
Building your own storage can beat cloud at massive scale
summary: Dropbox migrated off Amazon S3 to their own exabyte-scale storage system, Magic Pocket. Files are split into blocks, replicated and later erasure-coded across zones, with a sharded metadata layer tracking where each block lives.
title: Inside the Magic Pocket

keyTakeaways: Tail latency, not average, defines user experience
Deep observability: tcpdump → kernel counters → root cause
Edge/network internals (SYN cookies, backlog queues) matter
summary: A customer reported occasional latency spikes to Cloudflare's edge. This post walks the full debugging journey, from tcpdump and packet captures down to the Linux kernel's SYN-flood defenses and network stack, to find the culprit. A masterclass in diagnosing tail latency.
title: The story of one latency spike

keyTakeaways: V8 isolates are far lighter than containers
Hide startup latency behind the TLS handshake
Multi-tenancy via isolates, not VMs
summary: Cloudflare Workers use V8 isolates instead of containers/VMs, so code runs with effectively zero cold start. They even warm the isolate during the TLS handshake, hiding startup entirely behind the connection setup.
title: Eliminating cold starts with Cloudflare Workers

keyTakeaways: Active-active beats active-passive for failover
Cross-region async replication with eventual consistency
Regularly practice regional failover (chaos)
summary: Netflix runs the same stack active-active across AWS regions so an entire region can fail with users transparently served from another. Cassandra replicates data cross-region and Zuul routes traffic; they validate it by regularly evacuating a region.
title: Active-Active for Multi-Regional Resiliency

keyTakeaways: Replicate cache across AZs for resiliency + locality
Global cache warming and cross-region replication
Cache is a first-class tier, not an afterthought
summary: EVCache is Netflix's distributed caching layer (built on Memcached) that replicates cached data across zones and regions for low-latency reads everywhere. It absorbs enormous read volume and shields backing stores.
title: Caching for a Global Netflix (EVCache)

keyTakeaways: Idempotency keys turn unsafe retries into safe ones
Persist request fingerprint + response
Exponential backoff with jitter for retries
summary: Stripe's canonical explainer on idempotency keys: how clients can safely retry POST requests over an unreliable network without double-charging, using an idempotency layer that records and replays the first response.
title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

keyTakeaways: Dual-write to old + new, backfill, dual-read, then cut over
Never do a big-bang migration on live data
Verify old vs new continuously during migration
summary: How Stripe changes the schema of a table serving live traffic with zero downtime, using the classic four-step dual-write / backfill / dual-read / cutover pattern. The reference playbook for safe data migrations.
title: Online migrations at scale

keyTakeaways: Token bucket in Redis for distributed rate limiting
Load shedding: drop low-priority work first
Different limiters for different failure modes
summary: Stripe walks through the rate limiters and load shedders that protect their API, a token-bucket limiter in Redis plus request prioritization so critical traffic survives when the system is overloaded.
title: Scaling your API with rate limiters

keyTakeaways: A central authority can be simpler than pure CRDT/OT
Conflict resolution at property granularity (LWW)
In-memory doc state + change relay
summary: Figma's realtime collaboration isn't CRDTs or OT, it's a simpler last-writer-wins model on a per-property basis, coordinated by a central server that holds the document in memory and relays changes to all clients.
title: How Figma's multiplayer technology works

keyTakeaways: Vertical partitioning buys time before horizontal sharding
A routing/proxy layer hides sharding from the app
Colocate related data to avoid cross-shard queries
summary: Figma scaled a single Postgres to a partitioned, horizontally-sharded fleet. They describe vertical partitioning by table first, then horizontal sharding with a routing layer, all while keeping the application mostly unaware.
title: How Figma's databases team lived to tell the scale

keyTakeaways: Push heavy shared state to an edge cache
Lazy-load per-client data instead of full sync
Edge caches reduce origin load and latency
summary: As Slack teams grew to hundreds of thousands of users, sending each client the full user/channel state got too expensive. Flannel is an edge cache that holds this data near clients and lazily serves only what each client needs.
title: Flannel: An Application-Level Edge Cache to Make Slack Scale

keyTakeaways: Put a durable log (Kafka) in front of a queue for burst absorption
Decouple enqueue rate from processing rate
Idempotent workers for at-least-once delivery
summary: Slack's Redis-based async job queue buckled under load spikes. They re-architected it with Kafka as a durable buffer in front of Redis, decoupling enqueue from execution so bursts no longer overwhelmed the system.
title: Scaling Slack's Job Queue

keyTakeaways: Multi-tenancy + self-service for many internal customers
Pluggable storage engines behind one API
Operability is a first-class design goal
summary: Twitter built Manhattan, a multi-tenant, eventually-consistent distributed key-value database, to replace a sprawl of Cassandra clusters. It emphasizes operability, pluggable storage engines, and self-service for internal teams.
title: Manhattan, our real-time, multi-tenant distributed database

keyTakeaways: Caching tiers absorb the read-heavy timeline load
Hybrid fan-out for the timeline (push + pull)
Custom hardware/data-center investment at scale
summary: A tour of Twitter's infrastructure evolution, from a Ruby monolith to services, custom hardware, Manhattan, caching tiers, and the timeline fan-out, and the lessons of running one of the busiest realtime products.
title: The Infrastructure Behind Twitter: Scale

keyTakeaways: The append-only log is the unifying data primitive
Operating Kafka at trillions/day needs custom tuning
Replication = replaying a log; streams unify batch + realtime
summary: LinkedIn, the birthplace of Kafka, runs over 7 trillion messages/day across 100+ clusters. This post covers the custom patches and operational practices (their internal fork, tiered storage ideas, scaling brokers) that keep Kafka healthy at that volume. The append-only log as the backbone of a company's data.
title: How LinkedIn customizes Apache Kafka for 7 trillion messages per day

keyTakeaways: Encode shard id inside every object id
No cross-shard joins, denormalize instead
Boring, well-understood tech scales predictably
summary: Pinterest deliberately chose "boring" manual sharding over fancy distributed databases: IDs encode the shard, there are no cross-shard joins, and all data is denormalized. A masterclass in trading flexibility for predictable scale.
title: Sharding Pinterest: How we scaled our MySQL fleet

keyTakeaways: Modular monolith: boundaries without network calls
Microservices aren't the only answer to a big codebase
Enforce component isolation in-process
summary: Rather than break their Rails monolith into microservices, Shopify made it a "modular monolith" with enforced component boundaries, keeping deploy simplicity while regaining the modularity that microservices promise.
title: Deconstructing the Monolith: Designing for Developer Productivity

keyTakeaways: Partition by workspace so related blocks colocate
Many logical shards per physical DB eases future splits
Double-write + backfill + verify for the live cutover
summary: Notion sharded its single Postgres (holding every block of every workspace) into 480 logical shards across physical instances, partitioning by workspace id so a workspace's data stays together. Covers the tricky live migration too.
title: Herding elephants: Lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion

keyTakeaways: One uniform "block" primitive for all content
Recursive parent/child references model any structure
Flexibility comes from a simple, general data model
summary: Everything in Notion, text, pages, databases, is a "block" with a type, properties, and a list of child block ids. This uniform recursive model is what lets users nest and transform content arbitrarily.
title: The data model behind Notion's flexibility

keyTakeaways: Availability over consistency (AP) for the shopping cart
Consistent hashing spreads data + minimizes reshuffling
Quorums (W+R>N) tune the consistency/latency trade-off
summary: The paper that launched the NoSQL era: Amazon's Dynamo trades strong consistency for always-on availability using consistent hashing, vector clocks, quorums, and hinted handoff. The intellectual ancestor of Cassandra and DynamoDB.
title: Amazon's Dynamo (Werner Vogels / SOSP paper)

keyTakeaways: Inject failure deliberately and continuously so systems are built to survive it
Test resilience in production, not just staging
Automate failure so redundancy is exercised rather than assumed
Design every service to tolerate the loss of any instance or zone
summary: Running at massive scale on AWS meant random failures were inevitable, so Netflix decided to force them proactively rather than wait for outages. They built a suite of automated agents (Chaos Monkey, Latency Monkey, Chaos Gorilla and others) that deliberately kill instances, inject latency, and take down whole availability zones in production. This continuous failure injection made their services resilient by design and popularized chaos engineering as a discipline.
title: The Netflix Simian Army

keyTakeaways: Keep read-only reference data entirely in RAM to avoid network latency
Deduplication and compact encoding make large datasets fit in memory
Ship updates as deltas plus periodic snapshots for freshness
In-process data beats a remote cache for hot read-mostly datasets
summary: Netflix needed to distribute large read-only reference datasets like video metadata to many services with low latency and no per-lookup network cost. They built Hollow, a Java library that keeps the entire dataset in memory in a compact, deduplicated form and updates it via cyclic snapshots and deltas. This gave every consumer fast in-process access to fresh data while cutting memory footprint and eliminating remote lookups.
title: NetflixOSS: Announcing Hollow

keyTakeaways: Model data movement as composable sources, processors, and sinks
Change data capture keeps downstream stores continuously in sync
A managed streaming platform beats many bespoke pipelines
Schema awareness and governance are essential at scale
summary: Netflix had many ad hoc pipelines moving data between operational stores and analytics systems, which were hard to operate and kept data fresh inconsistently. They built Data Mesh, a general purpose streaming platform that captures change data and lets teams compose sources, processors, and sinks into managed pipelines. This unified change data capture and stream processing so teams could move and transform data reliably at scale.
title: Data Mesh: A Data Movement and Processing Platform @ Netflix

keyTakeaways: Peer-to-peer distribution scales better than a central registry for large blobs
BitTorrent style seeding turns every host into a source
Decouple origin storage from the distribution hot path
Fast image propagation directly speeds up deployments
summary: Distributing large Docker images to thousands of hosts saturated Uber's registry and network and slowed deployments. They built Kraken, a peer-to-peer distribution system that uses a BitTorrent style protocol so hosts share image layers with each other instead of all pulling from a central registry. This let images propagate across huge clusters in seconds and removed the registry as a scaling bottleneck.
title: Introducing Kraken, an Open Source Peer-to-Peer Docker Registry

keyTakeaways: Standardize the full ML lifecycle behind one platform
Share a feature store so features are consistent across training and serving
Support both batch and low latency online prediction
Treat models as monitored, versioned production artifacts
summary: ML at Uber was fragmented, with teams building one off pipelines and no standard path from model to production. They built Michelangelo, an end to end ML as a service platform covering data management, training, evaluation, deployment, and both batch and online prediction serving. This standardized the ML workflow and let teams across Uber build, deploy, and operate models at scale.
title: Meet Michelangelo: Uber's Machine Learning Platform

keyTakeaways: Purpose built time series storage scales where general databases stall
Downsampling and retention tiers control long term storage cost
A Prometheus compatible layer preserves ecosystem tooling
High availability and consistency both matter for monitoring data
summary: Uber's monitoring needed to store billions of time series metrics cheaply and reliably, which off the shelf systems could not do at their scale. They built M3, a distributed metrics platform with a purpose built time series database, downsampling, and a Prometheus compatible query layer. It gave Uber long term, cost efficient, highly available metrics storage for global operations.
title: M3: Uber's Large-scale Metrics Platform for Prometheus

keyTakeaways: Consistent hashing spreads ownership evenly and limits reshuffling
SWIM gossip gives decentralized membership and failure detection
Application level sharding can live in a library
Self healing rings tolerate node churn gracefully
summary: Uber needed application level sharding and failure handling without standing up heavyweight coordination infrastructure for every service. They built Ringpop, a library that uses consistent hashing and the SWIM gossip protocol so cooperating nodes form a self healing ring and route requests to the right owner. This gave services scalable, fault tolerant partitioning as an embeddable library rather than a separate system.
title: How Ringpop Helps Distribute Your Application

keyTakeaways: Define pipelines as code so they are versioned and testable
Model dependencies as a DAG for clear scheduling and retries
Built in monitoring and backfill make operations manageable
A good orchestration abstraction outlives the original use case
summary: Airbnb's growing web of data pipelines was hard to author, schedule, and monitor with existing cron based tooling. They built Airflow, a platform where workflows are defined as directed acyclic graphs in Python and executed by a scheduler with rich monitoring and backfill support. Airflow became the standard way to orchestrate data pipelines and was later widely adopted across the industry.
title: Airflow: a workflow management platform

keyTakeaways: GraphQL lets clients fetch exactly the data they need in one request
A shared schema reduces duplicated fetching logic across platforms
Standardizing the data layer accelerates feature development
Consistent data and presentation abstractions pay off at scale
summary: As Airbnb grew, teams duplicated data fetching and UI logic across web and mobile, slowing development. They adopted GraphQL with Apollo plus a unified data and presentation layer so clients declare the data they need and share code across platforms. This reduced boilerplate and let teams ship features much faster at scale.
title: How Airbnb Moves 10x Faster at Scale with GraphQL and Apollo

keyTakeaways: Sync correctness demands an explicit, well defined data model
Rust gave safety and performance for a critical client component
Randomized and property based testing catch deep concurrency bugs
A ground up rewrite can be justified when complexity blocks progress
summary: Dropbox's original sync engine had grown complex and hard to reason about, making correctness bugs costly across hundreds of millions of clients. They rewrote it as Nucleus in Rust, with a clearer model of sync state and heavy testing including randomized and property based testing. The result was a more correct, maintainable engine that they could evolve with confidence.
title: Rewriting the heart of our sync engine

keyTakeaways: Migrate incrementally with dual compatibility to reduce risk
Packaging and interpreter bundling are as hard as the code changes
Automated type and syntax tooling accelerates large migrations
Plan for platform differences when shipping to millions of clients
summary: Dropbox's desktop client shipped millions of lines of Python 2 code that had to move to Python 3 before Python 2 reached end of life. They incrementally migrated a huge codebase running on hundreds of millions of machines, handling packaging, compatibility, and a frozen interpreter across platforms. The migration completed with minimal user disruption, one of the largest Python 3 transitions ever done.
title: How we rolled out one of the largest Python 3 migrations ever

keyTakeaways: V8 isolates give near zero cold start versus containers or VMs
Running at the edge puts compute close to every user
Isolates pack many tenants per process cheaply and securely
A familiar language lowers the barrier to edge computing
summary: Customers wanted to run custom logic at Cloudflare's edge but traditional containers or VMs were too slow and heavy to spin up per request across a global network. Cloudflare built Workers, running JavaScript in lightweight V8 isolates so code executes in every data center with negligible cold start. This let developers deploy serverless code globally that runs close to users with minimal overhead.
title: Introducing Cloudflare Workers

keyTakeaways: A single authoritative instance per object enables strong consistency
Colocating compute and state simplifies coordination
Durable Objects unlock realtime apps like chat and collaboration at the edge
Stateful primitives complement stateless serverless functions
summary: Serverless functions are stateless, which makes coordination and consistent shared state like realtime collaboration hard to build at the edge. Cloudflare introduced Durable Objects, single instance addressable objects that provide strongly consistent storage and a single point of coordination for each key. This gave developers a primitive for stateful, coordinated, realtime applications on the edge network.
title: Workers Durable Objects: A New Approach to Stateful Serverless

keyTakeaways: Rust delivers memory safety without sacrificing proxy performance
Fleet wide connection reuse cuts latency and origin load
A custom proxy enables architecture changes Nginx could not
Efficiency gains compound enormously at Cloudflare scale
summary: Cloudflare's Nginx based proxy limited connection reuse and was hard to customize at their traffic scale. They built Pingora, a new proxy in Rust with an architecture that improves connection pooling across the fleet and gives memory safety and programmability. Pingora cut CPU and memory use and served trillions of requests while improving performance and reliability.
title: How we built Pingora, the proxy that connects Cloudflare to the Internet

keyTakeaways: Client-server SFU routing scales voice far better than mesh peer-to-peer
A shared C++ media engine unifies desktop, iOS, and Android behavior
Hundreds of voice servers across regions provide redundancy against failures
Decoupling signaling from media transport lets each scale independently
summary: Discord explains the client-server WebRTC architecture behind its voice infrastructure, serving over 2.6 million concurrent voice users. It covers why they chose selective forwarding units over peer-to-peer, and how a single C++ media engine across platforms keeps latency low.
title: How Discord Handles Two and a Half Million Concurrent Voice Users using WebRTC

keyTakeaways: One wide, structured log line per request centralizes the fields you need
Modules decorate a shared context that a final middleware drains into the line
Wrapping emission in an ensure block guarantees the line even on errors
Canonical lines complement, not replace, metrics and distributed tracing
summary: Stripe describes emitting a single wide, structured log line per request that aggregates the request's key attributes in one place. This makes debugging and ad hoc analysis fast without replacing metrics or tracing.
title: Fast and flexible observability with canonical log lines

keyTakeaways: Cross-tenant features force revisiting core partitioning and access-control assumptions
Messages must be stored so both workspaces can consistently participate
User visibility rules become conditional on shared membership
The Flannel edge cache had to be extended to represent external users
summary: Slack describes the architectural rework needed to let channels span workspace boundaries, breaking the assumption that a workspace is the atomic unit of data partitioning. It covers message distribution, cross-workspace user visibility, and edge cache changes.
title: How Slack Built Shared Channels

keyTakeaways: A hierarchical document model with transactions on related documents fits social data
MySQL as the storage engine provides reliability while the system adds distribution
Apache Helix plus ZooKeeper handle cluster management and partition assignment
A change capture stream enables downstream indexing and replication
summary: LinkedIn introduces Espresso, a distributed, fault-tolerant document store serving as source of truth for many products. It offers a hierarchical document model, secondary indexing, and a timeline-consistent change capture stream, built on MySQL and Helix.
title: Introducing Espresso: LinkedIn's distributed document store

keyTakeaways: Serving derived data needs a store optimized for bulk ingestion and low-latency reads
First-class ingestion of both batch and streaming outputs unifies pipelines
Eventual consistency and horizontal scalability suit feature serving
Venice gradually replaced Voldemort and bespoke serving systems
summary: LinkedIn open sources Venice, a high-throughput, low-latency read-optimized store for serving derived data from batch and stream processing jobs. It powers over 1800 datasets and most AI feature-serving use cases like People You May Know.
title: Open Sourcing Venice: LinkedIn's Derived Data Platform

keyTakeaways: A purpose-built C++ engine gave more control over latency and capacity than Lucene
A generic IR platform can serve many products, from ads to related pins
Inverted-index search extends naturally to approximate nearest neighbor
Incremental indexing keeps results fresh within minutes
summary: Pinterest describes Manas, an in-house C++ search and information-retrieval platform built to replace a Lucene-based system as query volume and index size grew. It powers search, ads, home feed, and related pins with lower latency and higher capacity.
title: Manas: A high performing customized search system

keyTakeaways: A tiered design separates hot recent data in memory from cheaper long-term storage
OpenTSDB-compatible APIs eased migration off the previous system
Purpose-built C++ storage cut cost and latency for high-cardinality metrics
A compactor aggregates and converts data as it ages across tiers
summary: Pinterest introduces Goku, an in-house time series database with OpenTSDB-compatible APIs written in C++, built to replace a degrading OpenTSDB deployment. It splits into short-term in-memory and long-term SSD/HDD tiers for cost-efficient metrics storage.
title: Goku: A scalable and high performant time series database

keyTakeaways: Idempotency keys prevent double charges when requests are retried
Timeouts and circuit breakers stop failures in one dependency from cascading
Load shedding and capacity planning protect the system under spikes
Monitoring and incident runbooks matter as much as the code paths
summary: Shopify shares techniques for making payment systems failure-resistant, since merchant livelihoods depend on uptime. It covers timeouts, circuit breakers, idempotency keys, monitoring, and incident practices for reliably capturing payments.
title: Building Resilient Payment Systems

keyTakeaways: Model the domain as objects (nodes) and associations (edges)
A graph aware cache eliminates manual glue code between memcache and MySQL
Read heavy social workloads are served from a two tier cache backed by sharded MySQL
Eventual consistency is an acceptable trade for global availability
summary: TAO is the distributed data store Meta built to serve the social graph of objects and associations for billions of users. It replaced the fragile combination of memcache and MySQL that engineers stitched together by hand, offering a graph aware read optimized cache in front of MySQL. The design favors availability and low latency reads over strict consistency.
title: TAO: The power of the graph

keyTakeaways: Use memcache as a demand filled lookaside cache in front of the database
Leases prevent stale sets and thundering herd stampedes on hot keys
Partition versus replicate pools based on request rate and item size
Cross region invalidation keeps replica caches coherent with the primary
summary: This NSDI paper describes how Facebook turned single node memcached into a distributed caching system handling billions of requests per second over trillions of items. It covers the engineering needed to scale a lookaside cache across clusters, regions, and data centers while keeping it consistent with the backing database.
title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook

keyTakeaways: Fallback code rarely runs so it is poorly tested and untrustworthy under load
Fallback can amplify a partial failure into a correlated total failure
Prefer making the primary path reliable over adding a secondary path
When fallback is unavoidable, exercise it continuously in production
summary: Amazon argues that fallback logic, the backup code path taken when a primary path fails, is often more dangerous than the failure it tries to hide. Fallback paths are rarely exercised, so they tend to fail exactly when they are needed most, and they can turn a partial outage into a full one.
title: Avoiding fallback in distributed systems

keyTakeaways: Set timeouts based on measured latency distributions not arbitrary guesses
Retries only help for transient errors and must be bounded
Exponential backoff spreads load after failures
Add jitter so clients do not retry in lockstep and overwhelm a recovering service
summary: Amazon explains how clients should handle the inevitable failures of remote calls in distributed systems. It walks through setting sane timeouts, retrying safely, and spacing retries with exponential backoff plus jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms.
title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

keyTakeaways: Focus on four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation
Separate the latency of successful requests from failed ones
Alert on symptoms that affect users rather than every internal cause
Keep alerting simple to avoid pager fatigue and noise
summary: This chapter of the Google SRE book defines a practical philosophy for monitoring user facing systems. It introduces the four golden signals of latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as the minimum set of metrics worth alerting on, and distinguishes symptom based from cause based alerting.
title: Monitoring Distributed Systems: The Four Golden Signals

keyTakeaways: TrueTime bounds clock uncertainty using GPS and atomic clocks
External consistency lets transactions be ordered globally by timestamp
Two phase commit and Paxos provide fault tolerant replicated transactions
Waiting out the clock uncertainty interval guarantees correct commit ordering
summary: Spanner is Google's globally distributed database that provides externally consistent transactions across data centers on multiple continents. Its key innovation is the TrueTime API, which exposes clock uncertainty so the system can assign globally meaningful commit timestamps.
title: Spanner: Google's Globally Distributed Database

keyTakeaways: Idempotent producers use sequence numbers to deduplicate retried writes
Transactions make writes across multiple partitions atomic
Kafka Streams composes these into end to end exactly once processing
The performance overhead of transactions is small in practice
summary: Confluent explains how Apache Kafka delivers exactly once processing semantics in a distributed streaming pipeline. It breaks the guarantee into three parts: idempotent producers, atomic multi partition transactions, and end to end guarantees in Kafka Streams.
title: Exactly-Once Semantics: How Kafka Does It

keyTakeaways: Move cold log segments to object storage while keeping a local hotset
Near stateless brokers rebalance and scale much faster
Object storage decouples retention from compute cost
An internal metadata topic tracks the location of remote segments
summary: This post introduces Tiered Storage for Kafka, which offloads older log segments from broker local disks to cheap object storage such as Amazon S3. By keeping only a recent hotset on local disk, brokers become nearly stateless, making rebalancing and scaling far faster and cheaper.
title: Infinite Storage in Confluent Platform (Tiered Storage)

keyTakeaways: A purpose built time series store handles multi terabyte hourly ingestion
Columnar storage plus LSM trees give fast analytical reads
Stateless nodes coordinate through a gossip protocol for horizontal scaling
Presto integration lets analysts use standard SQL over real time data
summary: Grab describes TalariaDB, a distributed time series database it built to query terabytes of real time event data per hour with sub second latency. Backed by an LSM tree store and a columnar format, TalariaDB exposes data to analysts through Presto.
title: Querying Big Data in Real-time with Presto and TalariaDB

keyTakeaways: Change data capture from binlogs avoids fragile dual writes
Debezium and DynamoDB streams produce events into Kafka
Ingesting from replicas keeps load off production databases
One pipeline serves analytics, disaster recovery, and audit needs
summary: Grab explains how its Caspian team built a change data capture pipeline to stream transactional data from MySQL, Aurora, and DynamoDB into Kafka in real time. Using Debezium and binlog based capture instead of dual writes removed data inconsistency and reduced load on production databases.
title: Real-time data ingestion in Grab

keyTakeaways: Change data capture with Maxwell streams database changes into Kafka
Separate pipelines handle real time entities and real time events
TimescaleDB, S3, and Presto serve different query patterns
Ordering guarantees and replica lag are the hard problems at scale
summary: Razorpay describes moving from batch ETL to a unified real time data platform as its payments volume grew to roughly 100 million transactions and half a billion events per day. It uses Maxwell for change data capture into Kafka for entities and an internal Go pipeline for events, landing data in TimescaleDB, S3, and Presto.
title: Building a Real-time Data Highway

keyTakeaways: A shard per core design removes cross thread synchronization overhead
A custom LSM tree engine is tuned for high throughput metrics ingestion
Aggregation buffers cut memory use for distribution metrics
Rewriting in Rust improved both performance and maintainability
summary: Datadog details the sixth generation of its real time time series database, a full rewrite in Rust that delivers a large increase in ingestion and faster queries. The design uses a custom LSM tree engine and a shard per core architecture that eliminates cross thread synchronization.
title: Evolving our real-time timeseries storage in Rust

keyTakeaways: An inverted index over every tag avoids full table scans
Search engine techniques apply directly to metrics indexing
Intranode sharding across RocksDB instances enables parallel queries
The redesign cut query timeouts sharply and raised cardinality limits
summary: Datadog explains how it replaced a query log driven index with an inverted index that unconditionally indexes every ingested tag, similar to a search engine. Combined with intranode sharding across RocksDB instances and a rewrite in Rust, the new system eliminated full scans for unpredictable user queries.
title: Timeseries indexing at scale

keyTakeaways: Ship code behind experiments that are disabled by default
Decouple deployment from release so rollout risk is controlled
Independent feature toggles allow surgical rollbacks
An automated circuit breaker halts harmful releases in seconds
summary: Booking.com describes how it uses online controlled experiments as the mechanism for shipping software quickly and safely. New code is deployed behind experiments that are off by default, so releasing code does not immediately change the user experience and features can be toggled independently.
title: Moving fast, breaking things, and fixing them quickly

keyTakeaways: Monoliths eventually block deploy independence and org scaling
Strangler fig migration replaces pieces without a big bang rewrite
Microservices let small teams own, scale, and deploy independently
Freezing the monolith to critical fixes focuses effort on the new architecture
summary: DoorDash outgrew its Python monolith as traffic and the engineering org scaled, so it moved business critical workflows into independently deployable microservices. The team used a strangler fig pattern to gradually replace the legacy system while freezing the monolith for critical fixes only.
title: How DoorDash Transitioned from a Monolith to Microservices

keyTakeaways: RabbitMQ and Celery hit reliability limits under heavy async load
Kafka's durable partitioned log absorbs spikes that broke the old broker
A gradual traffic cutover enabled migration without downtime
At least once delivery and horizontal scaling improved resilience
summary: DoorDash's Celery and RabbitMQ based async task system caused frequent outages that threatened order checkout and Dasher assignment. The team built a Kafka based asynchronous task processing system and cut traffic over gradually with zero downtime.
title: Replacing RabbitMQ with Apache Kafka Without Downtime

keyTakeaways: An out of process sidecar proxy standardizes networking across polyglot services
Envoy makes the network transparent and failures easier to locate
A single data plane provides discovery, retries, and observability uniformly
Started as an edge proxy then expanded into a full service mesh
summary: Lyft open sourced Envoy, a high performance C++ proxy built to make the network transparent to applications across a large service oriented architecture. Deployed as both an edge proxy and a sidecar, Envoy formed a mesh across Lyft services handling millions of requests per second.
title: Announcing Envoy: C++ L7 proxy and communication bus

keyTakeaways: Data discovery is a productivity bottleneck at scale
A search first UX over a metadata graph speeds finding trusted data
Usage and popularity signals help rank the most relevant datasets
Metadata cataloging also supports privacy and compliance
summary: Lyft built Amundsen to help data scientists find and trust organizational data through a search based discovery interface backed by a metadata engine. It surfaces tables, columns, owners, and usage signals so people can locate the right dataset quickly.
title: Amundsen: Lyft's data discovery and metadata engine

keyTakeaways: Real time serving unlocks fresher predictions than nightly batch jobs
Streaming features require a dedicated feature store and pipelines
Infrastructure is the critical enabler for real time ML
Migrate incrementally instead of rewriting everything at once
summary: Instacart moved from batch precomputed predictions to real time model serving and from batch features to streaming features. The shift relied on infrastructure investments including a serving platform and a Feature Store that processes terabytes of event data daily.
title: Lessons Learned: Real-Time Machine Learning at Instacart

keyTakeaways: Live video ingest needs intelligent global routing, not static load balancing
Splitting data plane and control plane enables dynamic routing decisions
Real time capacity and network signals drive routing and failover
Smart routing maximizes utilization of available compute at peak
summary: Twitch replaced HAProxy based ingest with Intelligest, a custom routing system that moves live streams from edge points of presence to origin data centers. A media proxy data plane at each PoP works with a cloud control plane that makes routing decisions using real time telemetry.
title: Ingesting Live Video Streams at Global Scale

keyTakeaways: A shared real time global state demands careful storage choices
Redis bitfields compactly stored one million pixel values
WebSockets pushed live updates to large concurrent audiences
Multiple caching layers absorbed massive read traffic
summary: Reddit describes building r/place, a shared million pixel canvas that anyone could edit every few minutes during its 2017 April Fools event. The team used Redis to store pixel state with bitfields, WebSockets to broadcast updates, and layered caching to sustain very high read and write rates.
title: How We Built r/Place

keyTakeaways: A single overloaded database cluster is a major reliability risk
Schema domains define safe boundaries for splitting tables
SQL linters prevent cross partition queries that block migration
Vitess enabled online table moves with no downtime
summary: GitHub's primary MySQL cluster answered nearly a million queries per second and became a scaling and reliability risk. Engineers introduced virtual partitions defined by schema domains, enforced boundaries with SQL linters, and used Vitess to physically move table groups without downtime.
title: Partitioning GitHub's relational databases to handle scale

keyTakeaways: General purpose search engines did not fit code search needs or cost
Ngram indices enable fast substring and regex queries over code
Git content addressing and delta encoding cut index size dramatically
Sharding keeps per shard latency around 100 milliseconds at huge scale
summary: GitHub built Blackbird, a code search engine written from scratch in Rust for source code across 45 million repositories and over 15 billion documents. It uses inverted and ngram indices plus Git content addressable hashing and delta encoding to shrink the corpus and index efficiently.
title: The technology behind GitHub's new code search

keyTakeaways: Managed cloud services simplified operating a huge event pipeline
Isolating events by type stops one stream from harming others
Prioritizing liveness over lateness keeps the pipeline healthy under load
Event data grows far faster than service traffic, so plan capacity ahead
summary: Spotify rebuilt its event delivery pipeline on Google Cloud after migrating off on premise Kafka, using Cloud Pub/Sub as the transport. The system delivers millions of events per second and hundreds of terabytes of data per day that feed features like Discover Weekly.
title: Spotify's Event Delivery: Life in the Cloud

keyTakeaways: MySQL schema changes and DDL became untenable at billions of rows
DynamoDB offered a managed path to scale media metadata
Queue based synchronization enabled a zero downtime cutover
Migrating hottest operations first reduced risk
summary: Canva's media metadata outgrew MySQL on RDS as schema changes on the largest tables began taking days and online DDL degraded live traffic. As media approached a billion assets, the team migrated to DynamoDB and used SQS queues to synchronize data during the move with zero downtime.
title: From Zero to 50 Million Uploads per Day: Scaling Media at Canva

keyTakeaways: Delivering to many unreliable third party APIs needs isolation and retries
A database backed job store beats queues for reordering and durability
Immutable append only tables preserve execution order cheaply
The system absorbs backpressure so failing destinations do not lose data
summary: Segment built Centrifuge to reliably deliver billions of events per day to hundreds of downstream APIs despite flaky or slow third party endpoints. Instead of traditional queues it uses a relational database with immutable append only tables to store execution order, enabling fast reordering without copying data across the network.
title: Centrifuge: delivering billions of events per day

keyTakeaways: A microservices first design was chosen over a monolith even early on
Kubernetes cut infrastructure cost sharply versus the prior scheduler
Linkerd handles cross language RPC, load balancing, and retries
Kafka's replicated log gives durable, replayable messaging for payments
summary: Monzo chose a distributed microservices architecture from day one to build a bank that is always available, scalable, and extensible. The stack runs services in multiple languages on Kubernetes, communicating through RPC with Linkerd handling load balancing, retries, and routing, and Kafka providing a replicated commit log.
title: Building a Modern Bank Backend
